utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away due to his personal urgent matters. This will continue during the entire week. Again, the Chamber entered into empty Courtroom I, that's why it was a bit delayed. The first witness today will be Mr. Djuric?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Through the Chamber's Legal Officer, the Chamber received the notice about the four paragraphs that is to be added -- that are to be added to his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I -- the last statement, the last paragraph reads like this: "This statement is made at the request of the Defence team of Radovan Karadzic and includes information that they are interested in. It does not purport to be a comprehensive account of all the events." What do you understand that paragraph to mean, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That paragraph was actually inserted at my request because there are other things that Mr. Djuric participated in concerning Srebrenica and that his troops were doing that were not of interest to us in subsequent days, and so I didn't want him to be -- there to be the impression that he was somehow concealing these things by not including them in the statement. So in order to clarify that situation, I suggested that he add the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While reading this paragraph, I will -- I was wondering how the Defence statement -- witness statement is drafted and prepared. Is my observation that the witness statement is drafted by the Defence team and when agreed upon, the witness would sign it? Is my observation correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The initial statement is taken in the field. In this case at the prison there was a meeting between our investigator and Mr. Djuric and he sent -- they prepared together the draft of the statement, which they sent to us here in The Hague. And then when we had our proofing with Dr. Karadzic and myself on Friday we added -- or discussed with the witness and added some paragraphs to it, thus producing the final statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is going to cover Mr. Djuric, Mr. Costi, is it you? Do you have any observation to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning. Well, my observation is that in fact this statement is a selection of what Mr. Djuric has testified about in prior cases, and I at least in part disagree with what Mr. Robinson said in the sense that that information related to those days that he discussed in his prior testimony that are not contained in the statement. This is a selection of some of the facts that the Defence probably believe are more helpful. There are other information that I would try to get from the information during the cross-examination, and that's why we asked for one hour and a half time for crossing, although the statement is only two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But among the -- those four paragraphs suggested to be added, actually only two paragraphs made their way to the statement, correct, Mr. Robinson? Paragraphs 21 and 22? Or I may have a wrong version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, the version I'm looking at of 22 paragraphs is the one that we're offering. I'm not sure -- I don't have the other version in front of me, so I'm not sure the difference between them. But we did add some paragraphs in the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, the changes made pertain to paragraph 1, where information about the prior conviction of Mr. Djuric were added; paragraph 14, the last sentence; paragraph 21; and 22. So it does relate to four paragraphs, but the only full new paragraphs are 21 and 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, in light of the timing of the notice and also the concerns I expressed, I would like to order that paragraphs 21 and 22 to be led live. Shall we bring in the witness. Mr. Stojanovic, if you could introduce yourself when the witness is brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the counsel assisting Mr. Djuric could introduce himself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Once again, Miodrag Stojanovic. Today I'm representing Mr. Mendeljev Djuric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Djuric, before you commence your evidence, although I take it you are already well aware of this, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have told you, Mr. Djuric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Both you and I should make breaks between my question and your answer and we should both speak slowly so that everything may be recorded in the transcript. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D09590 in e-court. Zoom in, please. There is also an English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, pay attention to the screen, please. On the left-hand side there is a version in Serbian. Do you see your statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement and did you sign it as well?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement accurately reflect what you stated before the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to read a short summary in English and then I would like to deal with some additions to the statements that we added during the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably before that, you are tendering the statement as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And there are no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So with the redaction of paragraphs 21 and 22, I wonder whether there's any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit -- we'll admit it into evidence. Shall we assign a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, statement number 1D09590 receives number D3903, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Mendeljev Djuric in July 1995 was an instructor at the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior special police training centre at Mount Jahorina. He was assigned to train persons who had been arrested for attempting to avoid military service. On July the 12th, 1995, he and his recruits were sent to Potocari, where they were tasked to guard the civilians from Srebrenica who had gathered there. They remained there until 13th of July, 1995, when the last bus departed. Mr. Djuric was unaware of any plan to kill men from Srebrenica. He was unaware that personal belongings and identification were being confiscated from men in Potocari -- at Potocari. He never made any statement to the effect that the men would no longer be needing their identification. Mr. Djuric has been convicted of aiding and abetting genocide in the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and has been sentenced to 30 years in prison. He has appealed that conviction. Mr. Djuric testified as a witness of the Prosecution in the Popovic trial here at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to deal with the paragraphs that were added. I would like to bring the statement back on the screen, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, to lead live does not mean that -- to show the document -- statement to the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I apologise. Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, did you hear of the existence of any sort of plan to kill POWs, men, civilians after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I never heard anything remotely similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have a feeling or did you personally intend to destroy Bosnian Muslims as a whole or in a -- their part?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I never had any intention that would in any way harm anybody, including Bosniaks or Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war during the previous 43 or 44 months of war, did you witness the existence of any plan of that kind? Did you see that anybody unlawfully killed people?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No, I did not witness any such developments. I was not aware of any such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know anybody from your surroundings who had genocidal intentions to eliminate Muslims as a whole or in part?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No, I was a member of an honourable unit, the special brigade of the Ministry of the Interior. None of my colleagues, none of the officers or members of that unit ever did any such thing or discussed any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment I have no more questions for Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Djuric, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, we just heard that on the 25th of May, 2012, the State Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found you guilty for aiding and abetting for genocide for the event in Srebrenica and sentenced you for 30 years. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, I would like to see with you very briefly what the state court actually said you did in relation to the event of Srebrenica. First the state court said that you commanded the members of the Jahorina recruit in disarming the UNPROFOR members at the entrance of Potocari, weakening their power, preventing them from protecting the people gathered in the UN base and the surrounding factories. Is it correct that the state court said this?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I hope that I managed to prove before the BiH court that the allegations of the disarming of UN members are not correct, but I would like to draw your attention, I would like to say, and I would like to answer your first question: Yes, I was convicted, but I appealed and I believe that my appeal is well-grounded. I have four possibilities or four reasons to appeal or four grounds for appeal, and we appealed on all four grounds. One of them was confirmed by the International Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg and they thought that I was right. So I expect that that first-instance sentence will be altered and much more favourable on my behalf, in view of the fact that the Court of Human Rights said that I was right in appealing.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: All right. Now from now on I would ask you to just answer my question if possible with a yes or no. We are aware of your appeal. Now, the state court at trial said also that you commanded the Jahorina recruits engaged in separating the able-bodied men and in their imprisonment in the white house. Is this what the trial chamber said?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The trial chamber, not the prosecutor, and I state here before you that I was not in a position even to see the actions that I was charged with from the position where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: We will deal with each of these issues in detail very soon. Third thing, the state court trial chamber said that you deployed the members of the Jahorina recruits along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road to capture Bosniak men; is this what the state court said you did?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The state court said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: The state court said that you commanded members of the Jahorina recruits as they executed men from Srebrenica at the Kravica warehouse. Is this what the state court said?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And finally, the state court said that you commanded members of the Jahorina recruits searching the terrain on the 17th and 18th of July to find the remaining men from the column, knowing that they will be executed. Is this what the state court said?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And today you're here to testify about these events?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Events that, as you said, you are appealing before the state court; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, it is true that you were the commander of the 1st Company of the Jahorina recruits in those days?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I was an instructor at the training centre. According to the systemisation of the Ministry of the Interior, I received the decision to become an instructor at the special brigade of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It is true that you were the commander of the 1st Company of the Jahorina recruits in those days?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: In the way it worked, the centre did not have those military forms, didn't have companies or platoons, no. It was an unusual group that appeared. The instructors were given an additional task, to discharge those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me read you what you said in the Popovic case on the 1st of May, 2007, at transcript 10793. "Yes, probably as one of the oldest and the person with the most experience, as I was appointed commander of the 1st Company. "And how many companies were there, sir? "There were two companies. "And who was the commander of the 2nd Company, sir? "A. The commander of the 2nd Company was Mr. Nedjo Ikonic." So there were two companies, two commanders, you were the commander of the 1st Company; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have just explained or at least tried to explain what was the fact and what you can find in the documents that I believe you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you don't mention the word "commander" a second time I think in your statement, and the draft statement we received said at paragraph 22nd that there was a selection of important facts that the Karadzic Defence selected for your statement. Now, the information that you were the commander of the 1st Company is not there. Is this one of the facts that the Karadzic Defence asked you to omit from your statement?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Believe me that I did not understand the question. Please could you be so kind as to repeat it, please. I don't think I understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- that company, did it exist from the beginning at Jahorina centre or was it composed when you were sent to the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that company existed when I came to Jahorina because I did not come with the other instructors at the same time; I came later. Since I was undergoing training in the Republic of Serbia, in Belgrade, so there is that part that the Prosecutor mentioned. Since I was one of the oldest people there, I was given the privilege to lead that group that they called a company. Otherwise, I came as an instructor and that is what I was according to the law and according to the rules that exist in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'll try to rephrase my question then. In your statement you did not say that you were leading, commanding, the 1st Company of the Jahorina recruits; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, throughout the proceedings against me in Bosnia and Herzegovina I claimed that I was not a company commander, rather, that I was an instructor and that there was a group of instructors there who were my equals, and we distributed our work amongst ourselves in order to carry out the work at hand in an easier way.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: But you just agreed that you were leading that company during those days in Potocari? Yeah?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And I try last time and then I move on. The fact that you were leading the company is not mentioned in your statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I'm really taken aback. I mean, do you mean this statement I signed for Mr. Karadzic when I was in contact with his Defence, you mean that part? I did not really pay attention. I cannot say now -- well, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can I just ask you the name of the investigator of the Karadzic Defence who contacted you and who took your statement?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Milomir Furtula. He is the investigator who came to the Detention Unit of the BH court and he brought the statement there for me to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So the statement was drafted when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, on the morning of the 12th of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to know the meaning "in part." Could you explain, Mr. Djuric? You answered: Yes, in part, to the question whether the statement was drafted when you saw it. Could you tell us in detail how your statement was drafted and signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman who came there who I did not even know, he, well, probably had instructions from the Defence how to do things. We talked and I wanted the statement to look a bit different, so that's why I said "yes," but not fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You just said you "wanted the statement to look a bit different." So the gentleman brought a statement drafted by the Defence team; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know how the Defence team drafted that draft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you have the conversation between the Defence team before you saw that draft.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Defence team? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Costi. But just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, the morning of the 12th of July you and your company were the first Serbs to arrive in Potocari; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I do not dare claim that we were the first; however, when we arrived there in the area where I was, I did not see any other military formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you explained in your statement at -- actually, in your Popovic testimony that when you arrived you got in touch with the UN, which is something you usually do when you go into the field; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a group of UN members under the command of a captain in the area where I was, at the position where I was. I think that his last name was van Duijn, I hope I am pronouncing this right. Since it is usual police practice in Bosnia-Herzegovina when you go out into the field for any reason, when you come across certain people in the field then you contact them and that is how I established contact with these persons from the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, apart from getting in contact, you and your unit did something more. You forced the DutchBat soldiers to surrender their weapons and you detained or otherwise restricted the freedom of movement of some of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber heard the testimony of Johannes Rutten, P03948, which at paragraph 47 describing when he was -- his freedom of movement was restricted, he said: "We stayed at that location for a few hours. The group included me, my ten soldiers, and the doctor that was with me. I saw someone that looked to me also as an officer, and later on he became known as the so-called Captain Mane. I have been shown a picture, P03956, on which I identify the so-called Captain Mane. I protested to him that we were held there and I protested to him that we had lost our equipment. He didn't even bother to look at me. He sent me back to the rest of the group. A few hours later when he came back, I protested again and I said that we could do nothing more there and that we had to go back to the compound. And finally, he said that he would go back and sent with my group two Bosnian soldiers to escort me to the compound again." So I'm asking you again: You and your unit took equipment from the UN soldiers and you restricted their freedom of movement; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Categorically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I was thinking to show you the images that you already commented upon in your -- Popovic case, but you have already said that you remember the name of van Duijn as the UN DutchBat you spent most of the time with. And you were talking to Mr. van Duijn through your interpreter, Mike, right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I think that it is my duty to say that this is not an interpreter. This is one of the members of the training centre who happened to know a bit of English, and then we used him in order to be able to establish this basic communication. However, he was not an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, in the -- you spent basically all the time, all day, with van Duijn; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Almost all the time, both days, the 12th and the 13th. I spent them with him while I was out there on the ground, with him or in his immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you talk very briefly in your statement about the boarding process of the civilians which you testified extensively about in your Popovic testimony. What you don't say in your statement is that you were in charge of the unit that was engaged in boarding the civilians in Potocari on the buses; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said and there's a reason why I didn't say that. This group of mine was not in charge of transport or loading. We had a purely police task: To provide security for a group of civilians who happened to be in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: But you did co-operate with the UN in boarding the people on the buses; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And this is what van Duijn said in his testimony in the Popovic case at paragraph 2290 -- I'm sorry, at transcript page 2290. "Q. And from where you were located, sir, who was in command of those soldiers and that process? "A. From my point of view, that was Mane." And at 2286: "Basically, the way it worked was that Mane told me how many buses or trucks were to arrive, were present, and so how many refugees could be seated in those trucks." So what you were doing in Potocari was regulating the process of boarding the civilians on the buses; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No. You know, that claim made by Mr. van Duijn that I knew of the arrival of the vehicles, how many vehicles, what kind of vehicles, et cetera, I absolutely had no communication with anyone from the Army of Republika Srpska from whom I could have received such information. The only thing that we did in that area from the beginning of the transport civilians were frightened. However, after a few vehicles left, this fright disappeared and then people wanted to leave as soon as possible. And then actually our first job occurred, if I can call it that, for Mr. van Duijn and myself, that we organise these people that we had there and in a way to try to channel people. Because if one or two buses, it is impossible for 500 persons to board those buses. In a way we had to channel them, create some kind of order, so that this would move as safely and as painlessly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, what you just said brings me to my next question, in fact, which is you said in your statement that you were there to protect these people. And at paragraph 16 you also said that nobody was forced to leave. But this is not true, is it? Muslim refugees had no choice but leaving; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: As for the choices, wishes, and aspirations of the refugees, I really did not know anything about that at that point in time. I was not informed by anyone and I had no information whether they wanted to go, how they would go, whether they would go, and so on, all these questions. However, the fact is that once the transport started, civilians who wished to go did go, and as a matter of fact they tried to leave that place as fast as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me tell you what van Duijn said on the freedom of choice of the civilians in Potocari and what you said on this point. "Q. Now, let's go back to when you first met Captain Mane. I believe you testified that he approached you and identified himself. Did he tell you why he was approaching you? "A. He wanted to know if I was the local commander of the United Nations at that position or outside the compound, and he told me that the refugees were going to be transported out of the enclave. "Q. Can you describe what Captain Mane's demeanour and tone of voice were when he told you that, sir? "A. He was very clear and he brought it as a fact, that the refugees were going to leave Srebrenica. He told me that 200 buses -- he mentioned the number of 200 were coming to pick up these refugees and he brought it to me as a matter of fact." Now -- this is the end of the quote. When you first approached van Duijn, it was already decided that these people were -- had to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Whether any kind of decision was made and what kind of decision was made, I really don't know about that. I did not take part in that and I was not informed about that. However, that someone did -- or that someone had to go, I don't think that that was the case. The only information I had - because I was a very low-ranking policeman in that area, I did not receive any information. However, my superior officer a day before the 12th and the 13th told me that I was to lead a group to secure civilians, that we were supposed to do police work, and politics and others would decide what else and so on and so forth. So as for these decisions and these things, I really do not have any information. Who made these decisions, how, none of that, at least at that moment I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please. I have been restraining myself so far, but there are going to be a lot of interventions in the transcript. In the -- in lines 3 and 4 that I was supposed to lead a group to protect civilians [In English] "Protect" is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm putting to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I intervene there?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, although you didn't participate in the decision-making at all, at certain point of time were you told by whoever that there would be -- that there would be 200 buses coming to transport the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as for the transport, the number of transport vehicles or any topic in relation to the transport, I did not have any information about any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, your task in Potocari wasn't about protecting; it was about expelling, it was about deportation. And this is, in fact, what the state court said, that you order and control the members of the 1st Company who participated in the acts of forcible removal of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: That's what the court said, yes, but I claim that I did not take part in any kind of forcible removal of civilians in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. Now at paragraph 13 of your statement you said: "Not for a single moment did I participate in separating the people in Potocari on the 12th or the 13th of July, 1995. I did not know that the men were being separated from their families while I was in Potocari. I was not ordered to separate the men." Now, this proposition is simply not true. In fact, you saw the separation, you knew of the separation, and in fact you co-ordinated the separation of the men in Potocari on the 12th and the 13th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No, no, categorically no.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So can I have P00667, which is a video, Your Honour, very short. I would like to show the witness the separation, since he has ...

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you see here the men -- maybe it's not there yet. Here we are. You will see the column of men walking. And we can just stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, these men had just been separated near the DutchBat compound on the 13th of July. Do you recall seeing these things happening?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No. At the place where I was together with van Duijn, next to him, at that place at that location, certainly there was no separation of anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: We will get there too. Now, you see the man on the left of the screen wearing a red cardigan, don't you? I'm not asking you to recognise him. Just, do you see a man with a red cardigan?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah, and this, Your Honour, is minute 1 hour, 11 minutes, and -- no, sorry. My mistake 1 minute, 11 seconds, this is the -- that's where we stopped the clip that the witness commented upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this man is Meza Efendic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number again, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this is a picture of a mass grave in Kozluk. Do you see that there is a body with a red cardigan?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I can barely see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, these are the remains of the same man, Meza Efendic. He was separated in Potocari, executed, and put in a mass grave. Now, the men separated in Potocari, like Meza Efendic, were systematically killed. Now, you don't recall having seen the separation because - and I'm putting to you - you don't want to be associated with this; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No. Once again, I repeat, at the place where I was, no separation was taking place. I am not claiming that apart from that place something did or did not happen. I don't know that, I did not see that, I cannot speak about that. However, the place where I was, it is certain there were no separations or any of these things that you spoke of just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I don't need the picture anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the place where you were and let me read you what van Duijn, the peacekeeper you spent most of the time with, said about the separation on the 12th of July. And this is his testimony on the 27th September, 2006, in the Popovic case. "A. The Serb soldiers behind my location singled out the Muslim men and they were put two along in front of houses without any facade, and they were put there to wait. They sat down on the lawn in front of the house and of course I questioned Mane why they singled out these men from the women and children. "Q. And what did Mane tell you, if anything, in response to your question? "A. Mane told me that they had a list of war criminals, Muslim war criminals, and that they were going to check if the person, the men they singled out, were on the list of war criminals, which they wanted to try for their criminal actions earlier in the war." So talking about the location where you were, Witness van Duijn asked you why men were separated, and you gave an explanation. You said because you were searching for criminals, for war criminals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I do not remember. I cannot say with 100 per cent certainty, but I do not remember discussing that topic with Mr. van Duijn at all. Now I would like to ask you something very kindly so that it would be easier both for you and me. I don't know how appropriate it is for me to speak now about the judgement of the BH court; however, I have to remind you that Mr. van Duijn refused to testify in the proceedings against me and I don't know why. All of these assertions he made here that are negative as far as I'm concerned, he did not make it possible for me to clarify this matter before the trial chamber. And now that we're discussing that case and I see that that case --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: -- before the BH court is highly inspiring for you --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm not discussing --

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: -- please, there is one fact there.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm not discussing that case. I'm talking about his testimony in this Tribunal. Now let me read you another passage of van Duijn in this court at transcript page 2289 on the 27th of September. He said: "The explanation from Captain Mane was that they wanted to search for war criminals, and although that was credible I objected every time there was a clear view of the Serb soldiers singling out boys or old men that were too old or too young to be soldiers. So I objected with Mane when the situation happened. "And in those occasions, Major, what would the result of your intervention be? "A. On all these occasions I objected with Mane, he would let the men go through and accompanied the rest of their family to the buses." So not he recalls talking to you about the criminal investigations, but he also remembers that boys and older men were separated, he would object to that, and you would agree with him that they should go with their family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I didn't speak to Mr. van Duijn about the topics you have just discussed. I never spoke to him about that, and Witness Mike, the interpreter, confirmed before the state court of BiH that all these documents concerning the separation were never anything he interpreted about.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: All right. Then let's continue to talk about separation but from a different perspective. You said in your statement that you were not ordered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Djuric, in addition to the fact that Mr. van Duijn refused to testify in your case, you wanted to say something further. What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to add that the trial chamber thought it necessary to admit Van Duijn's testimony but didn't think it necessary to make sure his presence so that he could testify viva voce, with the strange explanation that it would be too stressful for him. But given the fact that this gentleman is a professional soldier, I have my doubts about that and I think that the real reasons are different. Because other witnesses who testified before the State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina spoke about a totally different truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript is a disaster. I am holding back, but, for example, page 25, line 15, [In English] -- says I confirmed before the state court of BH that all these subjects concerning the separation were never ... and so on. And in 26, line 1, witness didn't say "viva voce," but he said that he -- they couldn't make sure his presence to be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but we could all understand the context. Thank you. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, time is running.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So let's keep talking about the separation. I would like to call 65 ter 25328A which is an audio. This is an audio of Jovan Zametica, a spokesman for Radovan Karadzic. [Video-clip played]. "Interviewer: Mr. Almeda, thank you very much indeed. And on the line now is Jovan Zametica who is the spokesman for Radovan Karadzic, the leader of the Bosnian Serbs. "Mr. Zametica, what you're doing there is simply inhuman, is it not? "Jovan Zametica: Well, Mr. Humphreys, I shall give you a good suggestion. Why don't you, for a difference, once begin to blame the UN rather than the Serbs. "Interviewer: Because it is not the UN who are separating men from their families, putting them on buses, and driving them from their homes. That's why. "Jovan Zametica: Well, I shall say that in that connection. We are separating the men from women, children, and the elderly for a very good reason. You may not know this, and I'm pretty sure you don't, but at the beginning of this conflict and throughout it, in the region of Srebrenica the Muslims carried out some particularly gruesome massacres of Serb civilians. They're well-documented massacres, and we simply wish to question those men to find out whether some of them may have been responsible for those massacres. "Interviewer: So that is why all the males aged from 16 upwards, including old men, have been taken from their family, not just a few, not just who those whom it is acknowledged, a small handful, most people who are there, the independent observers tell us, have been involved in the kinds of things you talked about, all these men? "Jovan Zametica: Well, we wish to carry out a thorough investigation, and if you are dissatisfied with my answer, so be it. I know of your anti-Serb attitude from our previous interviews. But perhaps we may move on to more substantial matters. "Interviewer: Well, before we do, let me just make the point that we take our information from our correspondents in the area, from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, from organisations like Medecins Sans Frontieres, Sans Frontier, who have no axe to grind. And indeed, from the forces serving there, the British and other forces serving there. That's where we get our information from. "Jovan Zametica: Well -- "Interviewer: They are not all biased against you, Mr. Zametica. "Jovan Zametica: For a change you could begin to get your information from the Serbs, but I know you're not interested in that. "Interviewer: Well, we could also get it from the Bosnian Muslims but we seek our information from independent sources. "Jovan Zametica: I'm happy to supply you with well-documented evidence of horrendous massacres carried out by the Muslims in Srebrenica region from 1992 to 1995. "Interviewer: What I -- perhaps you'll tell me what is going to happen to all of these men. Are they going to be returned to their families if you discover that they are not guilty of war crimes? "Jovan Zametica: Well, when -- when they -- when the investigation is over, they will be presented with a choice, either they stay in their homes in Srebrenica, no one is going to expel them from there, or if they so wish, they can go elsewhere, they can go to Central Bosnia or they can go outside the country. "Interviewer: And how long will these investigations take place, do you think? "Jovan Zametica: Well, I'm sure -- I'm pretty sure this is going to be a rapid exercise. "Interviewer: Well, you say 'rapid,' are you talking about days, weeks, or months, or years? "Jovan Zametica: Well, I -- I think it's a question of days, maybe weeks, but certainly no longer than that. "Interviewer: So we would expect that within a matter of weeks the vast majority of these men would be returned to their families? "Jovan Zametica: Correct. "Interviewer: And how will they get there because they've now been separated from their families? "Jovan Zametica: Well, they can go there by the route that's already been adopted to Kladanj and to Tuzla. I think many of them will express the desire to go abroad because they don't wish to live in Mr. Izetbegovic's" --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, what you just heard was broadcasted on the 13th of July in the morning while you were in Potocari. So we have Zametica, Mr. Karadzic's spokesman and Defence witness, who told the BBC that the men were separated from the rest of their families; right? This is what he said?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I said a minute ago, if I'm not mistaken, that it is not my claim that this never happened, but where I was and the people who were with me and those UN soldiers and Mr. van Duijn, we never did that nor was I in the position to see or to observe anyone in my immediate surroundings doing anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So on the 13th morning, they knew it in Pale, they knew it in London because the BBC journalist asked the questions having got the information somewhere else, but you in Potocari, right there, had no idea?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Just a brief digression --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'd like you to answer the question before the digression.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: -- I arrived around 10.00 or 10.30 at Potocari on that morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Costi --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- please let him continue. Mr. Djuric, what you're saying is that you knew but you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I said it may have been happening. I'm not saying that it was. I'm not saying that it wasn't. But I didn't do it with my men and it wasn't anywhere near me. When the Prosecutor says that this was known, I can reply that I arrived in Potocari in the early afternoon, at which time Mr. van Duijn and some other people were organising transportation, and that had been going on for some two hours before I arrived at Potocari, and I believe that you can find that in statements from 2007 and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: But you are saying that you did not know the men were separated. On the 13th morning you were there, you did not know the men were separated. It may have happened but you did not know; right? Is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Not that I am sure that -- that I was sure about anything. I didn't know. I cannot say what happened further away from me. I never saw anything like that anywhere near me, but I can't say what other people may or may not have been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you also just said that you arrived in the afternoon when the transportation had already started, but this is not your testimony, it's not even in your statement. You got there on the 12th, in the morning, before the transportation started, and you got there on the 13th, yes, when the transportation had already started but while you were there separation continued?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: It was well underway. I really don't know whether it continued or when it began because I didn't witness it nor was I involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me tell you what van Duijn said about the 13th, because it is the 13th that you are suggesting now that you arrived in the afternoon. Asked question: "Q. On this second day," 13th of July, "of separation and transportation, sir, who was conducting the separation and directing the refugees to the vehicles? "A. The Serb forces and Mane leading them." So even on the 13th you were there when the separation was taking place?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that I arrived in the afternoon. I said that I arrived in the late morning and the hour was between 10.00 and 11.00. You're confusing me, and for the fifth or sixth time you're trying to put words in my mouth, to the effect that I saw the separation or something else. I said at the outset that I didn't separate anyone, nor any other of my men. I didn't give orders to separate them nor did I receive orders to separate anybody from anyone else. I didn't know anything at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I forget, can I have the audio that we heard be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was wondering on what basis we would admit this through this witness, but in light of the Defence position the Chamber has no difficulty. Shall I assign a number -- shall we assign a number for that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25328A receives number P6467, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, in your Popovic testimony you said that you have never seen the white house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber heard the testimony from many witnesses about the white house, Kingori, Rutten, Franken, and others, and van Duijn who testified in the Popovic case said that he saw the white house, that Kingori told him about the white house, and this is what he said on the 27th September 2006: "I saw a lot of men crammed as the UNMO Kingori had told me, crammed inside a house and a few of them sitting just in front of the house. The whole house was basically packed with men, and in front of the house the whole front lawn ... was ... packed with a mixture of personal belongings, photographs, and also, as I saw then, passports from the men that were sitting inside the house. "... seeing those passports raised a question to me, which I also posed to Mane, that basically together with Miki had followed me from the first location, the water truck to the white house. And I posed a question to him, that if the explanation he had given me about the war criminals was correct, that the men would need their passports to prove their identity, to show that they were in fact not on the list of war criminals or differently. "Q. And what, if anything, did Captain Mane say to you in response to that? "A. Basically he -- he grinned at me and he told me that the men didn't need the passports anymore, which at that point made clear to me that there was a very dark future ahead for the men in the house - and in fact for the men that had been singled out also the day before." So, Mr. Djuric, contrary to what you said in your statement at paragraph 15, you told UN peacekeeper van Duijn that the men detained in the house did not need their passport anymore; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't speak about that with van Duijn at all. This conversation never took place between him and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, let's move to another topic then. At paragraph 11 you said that the evening of the 12th of July - and I read your statement: " ... one of the instructors sent his platoon along the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje ..." What you did not say at paragraph 11 of your statement is that the evening and the night of the 12th of July it was you and part of your company who were deployed to the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stated that on the 12th in the evening, following the orders of my superior, I took part of the men subordinated to me to the road from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje and we reached Glogova, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And over the night you said in a statement you gave to the Blagojevic Defence: "I visited each and every man from my unit positioned on the road in order to see what was going on." Right? You stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now this is another example of information that are not on your statement. It's not there because you were asked by the Defence to omit the detail that you were on the road yourself?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No, nobody asked me to do that. I don't know what was omitted, but I was at that location. I assigned the people to various places and I believe that I visited them during the night, but these are details that aren't so easy to remember after so many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And the same thing happened also the night after, between the 13th and the 14th of July, as you said in the Popovic testimony, in your statements, et cetera, and also there, and I read your statement at paragraph 18: "In the evening of the 13th ... my men were again distributed along the road ..." Well, actually you distributed your men along the road and you visited them two or three times to check what was going on; right?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you said you didn't catch a single prisoner in these two days?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can I have P02987, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this is a report signed by Borovcanin on the 13th of July. It's talking about this MUP unit being deployed on the Kravica-Konjevic Polje road. I'm not sure whether we have it in front of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: We don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to switch to e-court from Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Here we are, Your Honour, it's there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: If we go to page 2 of the English, still page 1 of the B/C/S, you can read that it says: "In the night between the 12th and the 13th this armed Muslim group launched an attack in the direction of Konjevic Polje ..." And then he concluded: "... we captured or had surrender to us around 1.500 Muslim soldiers. The number increased by the hour." So in the night between the 12th and the 13th, Borovcanin reports that they arrested around 1.500 Muslims. But your company didn't catch a single prisoner and you haven't heard of it -- actually, two separate questions. Your company didn't catch a single prisoner, did they?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: A minute ago when you asked me if we had taken any prisoners, I replied that I personally had not. Now I'm saying that my colleagues, my fellow instructors who were there with those people - because I wasn't, I only distributed them, I wasn't with them - they didn't report to me that they had done anything during the night and that they had any kind of contact with any army or that they had taken -- that they had arrested anyone. I have no information about that. I cannot say if there -- if these things happened or not. My co-workers and colleagues never informed me of anything similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric, I said that your task that night was not to secure Bratunac; it was mainly to capture and kill Muslims along the road. And I'll be more specific. In the early evening of the 13th of July, members of the 1st Company of the Jahorina recruits, your company, killed around 15 men who were detained on the meadow in the Sandici area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I have no information about that. I had no information at the time. During the trial before the state court of BiH, some such information was presented to me, but back then at the time I knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: [As read] "The prisoner that they have been surrounding -- surrounding in, they had been shipped by the bus, and very, very late in the afternoon/early, early evening, there was 10 to 15 people left. And if we have asked the question when the next bus is coming to pick these people up. And it was told to us that there won't be any more buses and that we need to get rid of them, we need to shoot them. "Q. Now, sir, who gave you this order to shoot these remaining prisoners? "A. That order came through the gentleman by the name of Aleksa. "Q. And who was Aleksa, sir? "A. He was a deputy commander of 1 Platoon. "Q. Okay. Do you remember who the company commander was for Aleksa's unit? "A. I believe that was the gentleman by the name Mane." So the deputy commander of one of your platoons in the early evening of the 13th of July gave the order or conveyed the order to kill the 15 men, prisoners, they had left in Sandici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I have no information about that. My activities on the 13th were geared towards Potocari and the task that I had been given on the 12th from my superior officer. On the road there were my colleagues, instructors; however, no information reached me of any killings. They did not inform me about any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: But you visited your subordinates, each and every man, in order to see what was going on. And also on the 13th night you went twice - this is what you said in your testimony - to Konjevic Polje to see the commander of the 2nd Company, Nedjo Ikonic, so you were on the road that night and that evening and nobody told you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it may be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I'm afraid your time is up, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid it is, but I was about to add that I would ask the Chamber to give me ten more minutes after the break to touch upon one last issue. And I'm sorry for not having asked before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you could ask for any potential extension in advance, not at the last moment. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00, at which time you will have ten minutes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you very much and I apologise for not having asked earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 19 of your statement you said that you did not know about any murder that happened at Kravica warehouse on the 13th of July. And in your Popovic testimony on the 2nd of May, 2007, at transcript 10828 you said that you heard about the event in Kravica much later. And you said: "I heard stories, gossip of all kinds, all kinds of talk that can be true or not ..." So my question for you is, first of all: When did you first hear? What did you mean by "much later"?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I believe that this applies to the developments in Kravica which happened on the 13th of July, 1995, things that happened in the afternoon when people who were detained there were killed. This is what this is about and at that time I stated that I had learned about all that only subsequently, much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: That's what I said "much later," but I'm asking you when if you recall. Is it a question of weeks? Months? Years? At one point you mentioned you heard from the media. When did you hear about the event in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you when that was. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your commander, Dusko Jevic, testified in the Blagojevic case on the 21st October 2003, and when he was asked when he heard about the stories at Kravica. He said: "It may have been the same evening. This sort of information spreads rather quickly. People talk. It's a comparatively small area. I think I heard about this the same night -- the same evening because people were talking about it." This is at transcript page 3239, 3240 on 21st of October, 2003. So you that night -- testified this morning that you were visiting your men deployed on the road to check what was going on. Your commander the same evening was informed that something had happened at Kravica, that actually the events -- the killing took place in Kravica, and you heard much later and you can't even remember when. How is it possible that you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: How my commander learned what information he got, I don't know. I can't testify about that. However, the fact is that I was involved in only one activity relative to Potocari, whereas my chief superior, the chief of the training centre, was free to move about wherever he wanted to. I don't know where he was. I don't know what information he obtained and who from. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: But the state court convicted you for the event in Kravica and it said starting from the evening hours of the 13th of July, members of the 1st Company continued the execution in the Kravica warehouse upon the order and under the control of the accused Dusko Jevic and Mendeljev Djuric. So it's not true that you did not know. In fact, you ordered the men, your men deployed on the road and to secure the Kravica warehouse, to continue the execution?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: The court decision is not final. In my appeal I explained word for word through the prosecution witnesses and through the defence witnesses that what the prosecutor claimed was not true. It's not right to claim that this is true. I stick by my statement that I didn't know, that I didn't have any information at the time, that I only got that information later, much later. I don't know when exactly, but it was much after the developments took place in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can I have P06378.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this document unfortunately wasn't on our list of documents for cross-examination because the issue was touched upon the witness -- the witness said -- you said: "I was a member of an honourable unit, the special brigade of the Ministry of the Interior. None of my colleagues or officers or members of that unit ever did any such thing or discussed any such thing." That was this morning at page 8, lines 19 to 21. Now, if you look at this document, this is a list of members of the special brigade who were convicted for events related to Srebrenica. This is a two-pages list and it includes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell the witness what this document is about first.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm just describing it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: The -- this is a list of convictions or plea agreements before the Bosnian state court of members of your unit in relation to the event of Srebrenica. It includes 12 names including yours. Now, is this the honourable unit that you were talking about this morning that didn't do anything during those days?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that he's misdescribed the document and it appears to include members of other units. For example, the first list -- number one on the list, Vaso Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: If I may respond, it doesn't because the witness said I'm a member of an honourable unit, the special brigade of the Ministry of the Interior, not just the Jahorina. This is what he said. And these are members of the special police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We admitted this, but who prepared this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I think -- I think the Prosecution, but I get back to you with an answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in putting the question, it's fair enough what document -- what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I was describing the content of the document, Your Honours. The source of the document, I didn't say it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's prepared by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I will have to check, Your Honour. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So it's not true that it was an honourable unit at least during the event in Srebrenica; right? Several of its members were convicted for crimes.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Please, sir, you are twisting things. I said that I was a member of the special brigade of the police of an honourable unit, and this list includes members of the training centre. These people were in training in the centre that had been set up by the Ministry of the Interior. Only few of us instructors were there from the special brigade. These are not my colleagues. These are not members of the special unit. These are absolutely people who are something else, who were in training and who may have become members of the Ministry of the Interior, but they would have hardly become members of the special unit of the police. I don't think that they would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Many of these person are not members of the Jahorina recruits; they're members of other detachment of the special police?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: You're right, there are some of those members; however, the list that you have just shown me is not that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sir, the last question for you: Mr. van Duijn testified that you were in charge of the deportation. He said you were in charge of the separations. He said you were in front of the white house with him. He said that you told him that prisoners wouldn't need IDs and passports anymore. And you denied all this, you disagree with every single point van Duijn has made on these matters?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: I stated, as far as I can remember, and I repeated it earlier today, that I was absolutely not involved in that kind of discussion with Mr. van Duijn. I don't know whether he had that discussion with somebody else, it is quite possible, but it was not me and this was confirmed by a prosecutor witness before the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was an interpreter. The only possible witness of that conversation. He was the one who confirmed before the court that he did not interpret any such contents in a conversation between Mr. van Duijn and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djuric, before Mr. Karadzic has some re-examination for you, I have this question. Shall we upload his witness statement D3903 before the redaction. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember having seen your statement on which you signed, Mr. Djuric? This is the first page --

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and the last page. This is your signature, Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly read aloud paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: "This statement has been made at the request of the Defence team of Radovan Karadzic and it contains information that they were interested in. This statement does not comprise all the aspects of all the developments."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I see three sentences there: This was made at the request of Mr. Karadzic's Defence team; it includes information that they are interested in; and it does not purport to be a comprehensive account of all the events. Could you explain to us what you meant by these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of July, two days ago, I met with the Defence at their request, at the request of Mr. Karadzic and his legal advisor, or rather, legal representative. We talked about my previous statements. They told me what they would be interested in and this is contained in my new statement, but this is a very concise summary. That's why I accepted that the statement should include this paragraph, i.e., that this statement does not contain all the aspects of the events because I already testified before this Tribunal and before this court and the court in Bosnia and Herzegovina and I had more to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would you have added to your concise statement when -- if it hadn't to be that concise?

utterances.speaker: MENDELJEV DJURIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to answer for a simple reason. The statement that I provided is voluminous and it contains a lot more answers to many more questions. It contains a lot more details about many more things. The statement that I first provided was given on 200-plus pages, and also the transcript from the Popovic case when I testified in 2007. My testimony was over a period of one day and a half or two days, so I spoke at much greater length. And now after everything that happened before the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm sure that there would be even more to say, but I don't know whether that information would be relevant for the case of Dr. Karadzic. In any case, what they were interested in was included in the statement that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed, if you have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies. The cross-examination was not long, but could it be corrected by listening to the tapes because the transcript is very wrong. If I were promised that the tape would be listened to once again and the transcript after that is corrected, then I would not have any more questions for the witness and all that remains for me to say is to thank him for coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't help you in vacuum at this moment. They will do the routine review process at the end of the hearing, and if there's some translation issue you can raise it in writing, Mr. Karadzic. Does it mean that you have no question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Excellencies. But I'm concerned about the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Djuric. I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to be excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It will take just a couple of minutes to re-arrange because I've got quite a lot of materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I did notify by e-mail that the -- again, the issue of the path the re-direct is going to take I would like to be heard on, which should possibly be before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where are we in terms of the phase of the witness? We are to hear the re-examination or your --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we're going to re-commence the re-examination of General Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have another issue related to another witness that I would like to raise with the Chamber at this time. So perhaps while Mr. Nicholls is moving we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the courtroom setting to be settled in again, I have one issue. We'll issue an oral ruling. This relates to the Prosecution's motion to augment Exhibit P4995, filed on the 25th of July, 2013. In the motion, the Prosecution seeks to augment the expert report of Witness Dr. Ewa Tabeau, admitted as P4995, with the complete text of a table that was only included in part in the original report. Also on the 25th of July, 2013, the accused informed the Chamber via e-mail that he concurs with the motion and will not file a response. The Chamber notes that P4995 only contains the first page of a five-page table and is thus satisfied that the remaining four pages of the table available in e-court under 65 ter number 1D5517 shall be added to P4995. The motion is thus granted. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This relates to a witness who's going to testify possibly tomorrow or Wednesday and that's Franc Kos. Mr. Kos is currently serving a sentence in Bosnia-Herzegovina and arrived on Thursday, the 25th of July, at the United Nations Detention Unit. However, he has been kept in solitary confinement for the entire duration of his stay here and we're concerned that he may not be in a position -- in a shape to testify if that situation continues. I raised that with the commander of the Detention Unit on Friday when we were there doing the proof, and his lawyer Slobodan Zecevic also took it up with him, but they were not able to solve that problem with the solitary confinement continues today I'm informed this morning. So I would ask that the Chamber inquire of the UNDU for the reasons for the solitary confinement as the commander refused to share that with me and to take steps to review whether or not that is necessary, so that when we come to his testimony he's able to give it under good conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, I would like to go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But -- yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And again, good morning. Before we move on, I just wanted to try to clarify what is going to happen next in the continuation of the re-examination. Mr. Robinson sent this e-mail that he copied the Trial Chamber staff on Friday morning of a list of topics that he intends to go into or that Mr. Karadzic intends to go into during the re-examination. And five of those, in my submission, are clearly outside the scope of what's permissible from -- as arising from my cross-examination and do not arise from my cross-examination in any normal sense of the word. I did some very quick legal research on this, and I won't go through the cases, but it's an established principle that goes well back that the permissible questions to be asked on re-direct or re-examination are those that arise out of the cross-examination. That goes back to 1820 in a case I found in the UK and I won't go into the cases unless we need to. But I just want to be clear on what I see happening here and why this is -- it would be a mistake to go down that road. The Defence's only argument or ground to allow them to go through this exercise is that the Prosecution asked factual questions of their witness who was called as an expert. And I frankly think it's a tactical decision and a rather cynical one.
