Because first they chose to call Mr. Keserovic as an expert witness, even though his three prior testimonies before this Chamber have all been factual and based largely on his Srebrenica participation. That may have been due to trying to avoid the appearance of calling as an expert witness somebody who was deeply involved in the conflict, the same thing that prevented him from being appointed as an investigator on this case. But they've cited no law and that's probably because this doesn't come up. Most times when somebody calls an expert who they want to say is impartial and objective, it's not somebody who's been involved in exactly the subject matter of their report. And Mr. Robinson basically started to concede this point when we were talking about it last Thursday at T42029. He said: "But we decided not to ..." And then he stopped and said: " ... it would not have been proper for us to elicit questions from an expert witness." And he said: "So once his role in the facts of the case are open, then we think it's a different situation, simply the scope of re-examination -- or re-direct examination for a fact witness -- for someone who is here as a fact witness from the beginning ..." And again, there's no legal basis for that because they could have called him as a fact witness in direct from the beginning and there's no basis that cross-examining him on his -- on factual issues somehow negates the normal rule of the proper scope of re-direct. And one thing I think is important is for Mr. Robinson's e-mail, and I think they will agree, that it appears clear that they spoke to Mr. Keserovic about what his testimony will be about Srebrenica events, that they essentially proofed him on what topics would be gone into on re-direct if the door was "opened" by me, because they said what he will say about reporting to the president, they will say -- they say what he will say about the practice of the VRS regarding identifications taken from prisoners. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the practice they would like you to adopt is that a party can adopt an expert who is also a participant and a fact witness; proof that witness and speak to them about factual issues; and then lead that new factual evidence without any constraints from the normal scope of cross-examination simply because they listed the witness as an expert. And that would, in practice, force the opposing party to decide whether to cross-examine on a pertinent factual issue, either one that goes to credibility or one that advances the case, knowing that they would thereby in theory open the door to an entirely new direct. That the basic rule is direct examination, cross-examination, re-direct, it's not and it shouldn't be direct examination, cross-examination, re-direct, direct, and then another cross, which is their proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene you, Mr. Nicholls. To understand you correctly, you are not opposing to the Defence putting questions with respect to those that arose from your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour. I just think that that is what the limit should be. Of course, everything to do with witness testimony and order is within your discretion, but it's a sound rule that re-examination is limited to clearing up and dealing with issues that arise directly on cross-examination, not - as they would have it - simply due to the fact that the witness was originally called as an expert, there's an exception that allows him to now go into any factual issue they like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, we take the position that all of the proposed re-examination deals with matters that arise from the direct, so that's one point. And we could deal with that on a point-by-point basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just, let's pause there. Mr. Nicholls, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If that's their position, fine. That's not what was said last Thursday and I'll object to where I think they're going beyond the scope and we can deal with it then. I just wanted to make sure before we advanced that we were, as I think Mr. Robinson now agrees, we're continuing with the normal rule that their questions must arise out of the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If that's the intention of the Defence, all this discussion may be moot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's our intention; however, if you find that something is beyond the scope, then we would still have the issue to determine as to whether or not we would be allowed to go beyond the scope. But I think we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There -- I see the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is the issue I would like now to resolve. And if Mr. Robinson believed - and this is not any kind of a criticism - if he believed that all of the questions on re-examination were going to arise from the cross and would be within the scope, then it's strange to send an e-mail of topics and thereby give "notice" of what the cross will be about. That's not usually done with re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think the Chamber probably already realises this, but notice was given so that in the event that any of the topics were found to be outside of the scope of the cross-examination, the Prosecution would have ample notice and time to prepare so that those topics might still be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if you like to respond to the general argument in Mr. Nicholls' submission, it's time for you to do it -- to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Our position is that this is a situation that calls for a different rule than what is applicable to normal fact witnesses, and that is because we called this as an expert -- this witness as an expert, and as such we weren't allowed to go beyond that framework of expert testimony. We could have decided to call him as a fact-plus-expert witness, but we didn't do that, so we decided to call him only as an expert. Therefore, we were limited to not asking him questions about Srebrenica and that was a choice that we made. And we told the Prosecution that if they were to go into that topic, we would expect to also address issues about Srebrenica that may or may not be within the scope of their cross-examination. And so they decided to go ahead and ask questions about Srebrenica to attack the credibility of the witness and also to advance their case. Having done that, we believe that we're entitled to go beyond the scope, the narrow scope, of cross-examination and have -- as if we had now the first opportunity to question this witness on factual issues. So we believe that because of the fact that this is an expert witness as opposed to a fact witness, that the rule has to be broader so that we can now have the opportunity to examine him on factual matters that we didn't otherwise have when he first testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You wanted to add anything, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. This is -- first you will notice that there was no cite to any law or precedent because there is none. This is, I would say, a dangerous slippery slope of this exception that Mr. Robinson or the Defence is now trying to create. The huge glaring flaw in his argument is that they were somehow precluded from asking the questions, factual questions, of the expert. The only reason they were precluded is because, as he now says, it was their choice not to call him. And if a party decides not to call a witness as a fact witness, they can't suddenly amend that. That's the flaw. That decision is not changed and should not be amended by my cross-examining the witnesses on issues that go to his credibility and advance our case that they know in advance there's a 99 per cent chance the witness will be cross-examined on, because he's testified about that three times before and it goes directly to his participation in the Srebrenica events. So his argument would be: I can call an expert witness, not give any notice of factual issues, knowing that that witness is likely going to be crossed on factual issues, I can proof the witness on those factual issues, and then when the Prosecution triggers it, I now -- all the rules about my dead-line of August 27th, 2012, to -- or -- yeah, 2012, to turn over material are out of the water. Somehow the opposing party has to make the choice between creating a new fact witness or not cross-examining on an issue that is screaming to be cross-examined about. So the logic is flawed, it encourages a cynical tactical approach to calling witnesses. And finally, the notice Friday morning is not sufficient notice and it doesn't fit with the practice and the Court's orders of how we are to be told about what fact witnesses are going to testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Simply, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Nicholls' observation. Shall we bring in the witness. While he's brought in, if you could advise Mr. Karadzic how to proceed. If necessary, we will take a short break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's going to leave these questions to the end. So we can maybe go ahead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and take a break when we get to that point or we may reach lunch hour then anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, today we'll hear Mr. Karadzic's re-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked during the cross-examination about the return of the 6th Sana Brigade, about what happened before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. In your view, when did tensions start mounting and was this rightly assessed in the reports of Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tensions started during the first spring months already in 1992, although one could conclude, or rather see, from documents that some activities that were aimed at disrupting these inter-ethnic relations started already in 1991 through the illegal arming and the organisation of paramilitaries. In his report, Mr. Brown states that non-Serbs also obtained weapons and that they tried, as he says, to organise themselves militarily. However, he does not give due attention to all these activities, or rather, through his report in some way he minimises all of those activities, or rather, he believes that that is something small, sporadic, et cetera. So already in the first spring months of 1992, we have an increase in tensions in the areas of all municipalities, Sanski Most included.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 1D9328.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are unable to locate the document under this number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue without the document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is a document from 1991. I would like to have it displayed. And could we now have 1D9329.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 6th Sana Brigade, what kind of situation did they find, say, in Sanski Most upon their return from the front line in Croatia? Was it idyllic or were there problems there as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation was not good. Inter-ethnic relations were strained. Previously we analysed a document that indicates that there was a different mood in the ethnic communities in relation to the return of the 6th Sana Brigade. So problems were on the rise, tensions were on the rise, and there were many differences and it was hard to resolve them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, there seems to be some problem with respect to the publication of those documents. The Registry can't locate those documents yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, Mr. Brown, did he establish and rightly assess and did you assess whether the army and police of Republika Srpska attacked innocent, unarmed civilians there or was there a military formation there of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were formations, military formations, armed formations there, of non-Serbs or basically Muslims. And they were asked to disarm, or rather, to return their illegal weapons and to continue to participate and resolve all disputes, or rather, to seek a political solution. I did not find any documents that in any way allowed or instigated or approved of attacks against the innocent population or any documents that indicated that pressure was brought to bear, that the population was under duress and that they had to leave the area. That is to say that the objective of attacks were military formations, or rather, paramilitary formations and disarmament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4282, could we please have that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we enlarge the Serbian version. I hope that there is a translation. Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is a document of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the staff of the Supreme Command, dated the 10th of September, 1992. And they're addressing the Una Sana Operations Group there. Did you know that this existed, or rather, which municipalities did it include?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Una Sana Operations Group included the municipalities in the valley of the Sana river, Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and municipalities on the Una, down there from Kulin Vakov, Bihac, Krupa, and Bosanski Novi or Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please focus on the second part of the first paragraph. It says: "I was even in a position to alert the government organs in that region that armed combat was being obstructed since they waited rather long. And while war was raging in all of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in this region they were still negotiating with the aggressor." Did Mr. Brown take this document into account and did he explain why in the Una Sana area the war started raging only after the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not analyse this in particular. As for municipal developments, for the most part he found the perpetrator to be on the Serb side. Allegedly they used small municipal incidents for all-out attacks and non-selective attacks, indiscriminate attacks against the civilian population inter alia. So he did not place into a context the efforts that were made to find a solution by way of negotiations, or rather, by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4282 receives number D3904, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now take a look at 1D9328. I believe that now it is possible. If it's not translated, I'm going to ask you to help us with a few paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look and tell the Trial Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a report from a meeting of the professional council of the security services centre of Banja Luka, where there was a discussion about the current security situation in the territory of the centre, that is to say the Krajina, and also information was provided about the mobilisation that was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when this was held and can you see among the participants any Muslims who were heads of public security stations, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is July, the 25th of July, 1991, that is to say a lot before the conflict broke out. We see here that Senad Dizdar is participating who is the chief from Jajce. He is of Muslim ethnicity. He was chief down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who's the first one on top?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziselimovic was in the encryption department and communications department, that is to say he was head of the department for communications and encryption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a word, this is a joint MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time that was a joint MUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina and thereby in the services centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Nicholls on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, no objection. I've just received an e-mail that there's a translation of this document under L0072838 is the ERN if it helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, when we could locate it, we'll use it, but in the meantime shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this kind assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, as for these conclusions, can you tell us about the first paragraph in your own words?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting resulted in a conclusion to the effect that the security situation is rapidly deteriorating in the territory of the centre and it is assuming the proportions of a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain where this dramatic deterioration is taking place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipalities are the border municipalities with the Republic of Croatia; that is to say, Bosanski Novi, Dubica, Gradiska, and Srbac. All of these are on the border; that is to say, the border towards the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the second paragraph here, for example, line 5 says: "There are frequent exchanges of gun-fire every day between the members of the special units of the MUP of Croatia, the members of the National Guards Corps vis-a-vis the settlements along the Una and Sana in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an increased concentration of all categories of armed uniformed persons in the border areas of Croatia, especially on the most frequent bridges."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We were doing a cite translation. We did not hear the question put by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, interpreters were not able to hear your question, Mr. Karadzic. They translated the citation, but your question ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this situation that is described here from July 1991, how was it reflected in Mr. Brown's analysis? Was it taken into account and was it sufficiently appraised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, just a suggestion. It's more helpful, I think, to cite Mr. Brown's testimony or report when talking about the parts that this testimony is in theory going to rebut. Just a suggestion because otherwise we need to look through the report to find exactly where this goes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Indeed that would be helpful when done either by the Defence, otherwise by the witness. Shall we continue this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try and say that. It is in the part that deals with the return of units from the territory of Croatia into the municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina. Here, in his findings, Mr. Brown did not in my view pay sufficient attention to the broader or external context of events and circumstances that lead to the spillover of conflicts and tensions from the Republic of Croatia into Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because we see that already in 1991 a danger was identified, namely, that these developments could spillover into the neighbouring Bosnia-Herzegovina. So when Mr. Brown speaks about these units, he is just moving them from this zone where they were used in Croatia into Bosnia-Herzegovina, but he does not deal with the transfer, or rather, the effect of what was happening in Croatia on Bosnia-Herzegovina. He just touches upon that briefly and then transfers units from one zone into another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution challenged your position that the 1st Krajina Corps and the authorities had a different attitude towards armed Serbs than armed Muslims and Croats. And they say that they were not prosecuted, I mean armed Serbs, as much as others were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We have a small technical problem. Just a second. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, General, where were you at the time and what insight did you have? I don't mean as a fact witness but as an expert. Were you familiar with this aspect of life in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in 1991, I was commander of the military police battalion of the 3rd Military District and I was leaving for the General Staff academy of the JNA in Belgrade for training. My family stayed in the Krajina and those summer months before open armed conflict broke out in Croatia, I stayed in Banja Luka, that is, in my place of birth, between Banja Luka and Prijedor. I was in that area and throughout that time I was in a position to see and live through everything and know how people lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on the last paragraph and do recount it. It says here that a group from Knin returned to Prnjavor and so on. Who were these persons? To which ethnicity did they belong? Who are being criticised here and of whom it's said that they committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doubtlessly for the most part refers to forces or some groups that until then had been active in the Republic of Srpska Krajina. It says here that they were members of Martic's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They are individuals with a criminal record; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are the ones mentioned in the last paragraph Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending English translation -- just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. I just apologise. I made a mistake before when I said it was translated. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it was a different one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D9328 receives number D3905, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now get 1D9329.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you establish when the 9th Sana Brigade returned to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the relevant documents on me, but I believe they returned in early April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at what the radio station and the public security station of Sanski Most were reporting about on the 6th of December, 1991. Maybe you can -- we can focus on these bullet points. Four explosions in Serbian-owned businesses are mentioned here. Please recount this to us, give us a summary.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report of the public security station of Sanski Most. Events are listed in chronological order that led up to attacks against property owned by Serbs. They mention nine cases here and each individual case is being described in detail including the persons involved and the items involved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here Muslim-owned property is also mentioned. We see these names: Mirnes Dzafic, Kaliman Kalic [phoen]. Are these Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then we see Nusret Ibrisagic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Difficult to follow. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just -- I'm not clear on what we're looking at. It's a MUP report or it's something to do with the radio? And they were both mentioned in the question. It's a radio report of a police report or just what are we looking at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we see the first page again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a report of the public security station of Sanski Most which was distributed to the media so that the public knows what is happening in the municipality in order to prevent similar events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the second page we read the following names: Hajrudin Alagic, what could his ethnicity be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniak, Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Natasa Sijan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sijan could be a Croatian family name, but based on the first name we could also suppose she was a Serbian woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see in the second paragraph that in two cases persons of Serbian ethnicity and three cases of Croatian ethnicity and four Muslim ethnicity are involved, which leads to a conclusion that the motives most probably are not ethnically -- of ethnic nature. How did you understand the statements and the acts of the Crisis Staff members, for example, Mr. Posara [phoen] in the context of these events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ewan Brown never dealt with these events in 1991. If he did, then he only linked it to some activities of the Serbs in a casual manner. Efforts were made to overcome differences peacefully. There were people who understood what this was leading and that there would be an escalation involving uncontrolled behaviour in the area leading to open conflict which eventually did happen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D9329 receives number D3906, Your Honours, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we're still dealing with the allegation of the Prosecution that you wrongly established that the authorities were lenient towards the armed Serbs. Let us look at document 25861. While we're waiting, you were interrupted, General, when you spoke about the establishment of Serbian defence forces or whatever they were called in the Krajina. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on All People's Defence included an obligation of the municipalities to actively take part in efforts and integrate the efforts of all stakeholders in order to face the current problems in a context of imminent threat of war or war time. Given the problems that existed, Serbian defence forces were organised. They were not special formations, specially created for that purpose, because there was the Territorial Defence already and there were municipal staffs of All People's Defence and Territorial Defence. All these units were integrated to try to cope with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain to the Trial Chamber what this document is and what the ethnicity of this detained person mentioned in lines 1 and 2 was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, just -- I didn't want to interrupt the question and answer, but just for some precision to know what we're talking about, at 68, line 7, when Mr. Karadzic spoke about the establishment of "Serbian defence forces or whatever they were called," are we talking about the SOS or just Serbian defence forces meaning everything, TO? I don't know what he's talking about. There is a -- SOS is Serbian defence forces, that's what I asked him about, in Sanski Most. I just want to know if that's what we're talking about because he said "whatever they're called."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will clarify. This document mostly deals with renegades and Serbian elements that were out of control, and we'll get to the SOS. They were present in Banja Luka and at Sanski Most and then we'll see what the General found in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us now what this document is and who this first detained person was and then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an official note about the placing in detention of a Serb who assumed the right to take care of some matters at a check-point. He was implementing some rules of his own in the area. The MUP or actually the SUP was -- the SUP reacted and placed him in detention because he was breaking the rules that were in force in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 14 we see a certain Serb was not recorded because you said "Serb," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read out the last-but-one paragraph starting with Lukac states. Can you read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Lukac states that this is about a group that was kicked out of the 6th Krajina Brigade and they procured weapons for themselves, rifles, pistols, Zoljas, and Osas, and they also have a hand-held rocket-launcher. With another group that was at Podlug, whereas these one were at Sivlik [phoen], at the check-point they started shooting together so that there was shooting from all around. And Solvi [phoen] with his group shot -- fired at a mosque from a hand-held rocket-launcher. The same group is in possession of a significant amount of explosives too."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, again, we've just sent a translation to the Defence. If Mr. Karadzic wants to bring it up and use it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, what kind of attitude prevailed against Serbian renegades or armed Serbs who were not members of official forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document which shows that the authorities, which is in this specific case the police, acted against those who were in possession of illegal weapons irrespective of their ethnicity. These persons here are Serbs. They were kicked out of the brigade because they were undisciplined, they procured weapons, but they were being arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document. Now we also have a translation by courtesy of Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you also confirm the date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't have the time to confirm that that is the translation, but I take the words from the Prosecution. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D25861 receives number D3907, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you had no objection to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, Mr. Karadzic, shall we have a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we commence, can I make or address a quick housekeeping matter. On the 17th of July, the Trial Chamber asked the -- or ordered the Office of the Prosecutor to liaise with the Rule 70 provider. I'm having some difficulty reaching the contact person -- not technically but in a manner that allows for meaningful discussion because that person is actually on the road. If we could have an extension until Friday, I'm optimistic that I could make the requisite contact and of course if we're able to do so sooner, we'll file sooner. And, Mr. President, I spoke with Mr. Robinson and he agrees with that and he has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. It will be so extended, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you were shown diaries, or rather, diary entries made by Rasula, perhaps Vrkes, Anicic, Vrucinic, and some others, and you didn't agree that their attitude towards Muslims and Croats was discriminatory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at 65 ter 20382.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not trying to interrupt, just it may have been a translation, but just for precision with the transcript. The diary entries were by two persons, Rasula and Davidovic. There were no diary entries made by Vrkes, Anicic, and Vrucinic. Only two diaries. So whatever entries weren't made by those other people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could agree. However, those people were mentioned as authors of orders and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, please look at the document in front of you. The executive Executive Board and its emergency session of 10 November 1992, and then you see the names of the people who attended the meetings, the most responsible people in the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the most responsible people in the municipality. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Serbian language I'm interested in the following page, paragraph 5. I believe that the English page can stay as is. Could you please tell us how this tallies with what you know. It says here together with the 6th Krajina Brigade Command, the police are instructed to launch a joint effort to disarm persons who carry arms and who are not members of the brigade. Does this apply to the Serbs? Who was allowed to carry arms without being a member of the 6th Sana Brigade or had been members and left it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning the position was to disarm all those who had weapons and were not members of the legal forces, i.e., units or the brigade or the police. Here I suppose that this applies to the Serbs who had weapons and were prone to committing various crimes. An order was issued for these arms to be confiscated, although in the paragraph itself this is not expressly mentioned, ethnic affiliation is not mentioned. When orders were issued to disarm people, there was never segregation according to ethnicity. The order usually or always applied across the board to all those who had weapons and were not members of legal armed forces. Given the author of the document, I'm sure that this applies to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up a little, that's for the Serbian page and in English can we go to the following page because I'm interested in paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is ordered by paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously attempts were made to enable the functioning of the local community, i.e., the municipality. As far as possible an order is issued to set up a work unit or a work brigade because the Muslims and Croats mostly had work obligation. All the citizens were to be allowed to participate in winter sowing, i.e., they were to be allowed to complete the winter sowing of winter crops. This is part of the regular, everyday life of the population. The times were hard and there was need to sow the crops in order to be able to harvest later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page in Serbian and can we scroll up the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 16 and tell us what it means. Are representatives of the Muslim community among these names?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 16 is the appointment of a committee for the distribution of humanitarian aid in the municipality. A certain Husnija Alagic, who was a Muslim, was appointed as one of the members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who signed this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then-president of the Executive Council, Mr. Vlado Vrkes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3908, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 65 ter 4223.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is and when it was issued.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was issued on the 6th of December, 1992. It is a combat report by the command of the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the last sentence describing the losses.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four dead and 15 wounded, of who two seriously wounded and 13 slightly wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page, both in Serbian and in English. I'm interested in paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude towards killings and crimes in the Krajina Corps? Your position was that it was objective and that everything was done by the book. Can you please tell us what is described in paragraph 5 under the title "unusual incidents"? Can you first read and then can you give us a short account.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen this document before. The paragraph describes some places within the municipality of Sanski Most where killings happened. Seven people of Croatian origin were killed and one was wounded. Among the killed were also some women. Two civilians were from Sasina, they were killed at Tomasici and in Sasina. This is a report about the perpetrators of the crime who were motivated by revenge as assumed. This man, Gvozden, who was a member of their group, had a brother killed a few days before. The corps command reports that the investigation was under way and that as soon as the perpetrators were identified measures would be taken against them and a report on that would follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D3910, Your Honours. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And not a similar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D3909.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9327 describes a similar if not the same case; however, the dates are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that you were asked about a crime that was committed by Danilusko Kajtez; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D9327.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9327.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We seem to have a problem again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It hasn't been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll work on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here it is. Here we have it. This is the document. Can we zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber something about this report.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information about multiple killings and those happened in the villages of Skrljevita and Kijevo. The victims of those crimes are described as well as the way those people were murdered by unknown males, as it is stated in here. In the first case which happened in Skrljevita, it is Croats who were killed, whereas in Kijevo the persons who were killed were two females who were of Muslim ethnicity. They were also killed by persons wearing uniforms. And it was assumed that the killings were committed by a Serb, Lazar Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at line 9 where it says Grgo Stojic who stayed alive, and a bit further down it says that three persons wore uniforms and one was in civilian clothes. They all had weapons. He didn't recognise them but was able to provide a description of those lads. On that day, Croats from the village of Skrljevita went to the green market. It was a Monday and so on and so forth. Did you know that Croats lived in those villages and that they had their teachers, that they had telephone lines, that they remained living there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Croats were mostly not involved in the conflict in a majority of the municipalities including Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked why Danilusko Kajtez was tried after the war. Based on what criminal reports were trials organised after the war? According to what you know, when were those criminal reports prepared and based on what information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to documents, the investigation against Kajtez was carried out immediately after the crimes happened, after the murders he had committed. The proceedings were launched against him. War crimes and similar crimes do not have a statute of limitations. I suppose that the general conditions under which the judiciary bodies worked at the time contributed to the fact that the proceedings were completed only after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you found in the documents and what you know, can a trial go on if the only eye-witness is not available to the court? What is done in such cases?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure this is a question for the witness. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That would have been my second objection. The first one is Kajtez was not tried, charged, anything with -- or later perhaps, but he was not charged with war crimes. He was charged with murder during the events. And I would like to know what document we're looking at on the screen which hasn't been said yet, what it's from and what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the ERN number further down. I received this from the documents that the Prosecution has available. Could we zoom out so that we see the ERN number. Yes, yes, here it is and the number down there is correct too. So probably there are a few more pages, but I haven't received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My understanding is that this is an AID document, a Muslim investigation document. I don't know if this is being purported to be some kind of contemporaneous police report because I don't think it is. I'd need to check more on what it is on my feet, but I don't know what the representation is that this document is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's not acceptable then I will withdraw it, but I believe it will be of assistance and I also believe that it's a Serb document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us continue when you have some more -- better evidence. We can come back to that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, were Serbs duty-bound to respond to mobilisation? Were Muslims and Croats called up and did they have the same kind of obligation, or did they decide of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to federal laws that were in force all the way up until the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina, all were duty-bound to respond to mobilisation according to the mobilisation schedule and to participate in all situations, exercises, and in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the war did we require Muslims and Croats to join the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not duty-bound to join the Army of Republika Srpska, but at one's personal request some of them did join the VRS. There were even entire units, Muslim units, in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 4868. Let us see how the municipality of Sanski Most that is being dealt with in these two expert reports, your own and Brown's -- actually, 65 ter 4868. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report on the work of the Sanski Most Ministry of Defence department for the first three months of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have -- actually, could we have the next page now, Juta Pazula [phoen] -- Pakula [phoen] is verifying this, authenticating this. Can we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Help us with this, General, what does it say here that according to records, how many recruits were called up, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, and how many responded? Those are the first two tables that you have here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see that this right was exercised, that is to say that they were all called up to respond. However, this second table, this survey, shows that in most cases it was Serbs who responded. And the number of Muslims and Croats is minimal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These Croats and Muslims who did not respond, were they sanctioned in any way and would Serbs who would not respond be sanctioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats at the time, that is to say throughout the war, were not sanctioned for not responding to recruitment or being sent for military training. These are recruits that are referred to. Serbs would be sanctioned through the military police. For the most part, they would be brought in and sent to do their military service. They were duty-bound to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the fifth page in Serbian from this one. So count four and that would be what we need, and in English it's probably going to be the next one or two further ahead. Paragraph 3. Yes, we have it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 3, the second sentence, also --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units for work obligation of Muslims and Croats have been formed in the area of town and three platoons with a total of 58 members and two platoons with 45 members in Majdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was work obligation compulsory for Serbs who were unfit for combat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, work obligation is a general obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3910, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 5120.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what this document is from July 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a biannual report of the public security station from Sanski Most, and it's sent to the security services centre in Banja Luka. It has to do with their work during the first six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please, I believe that it's the second page in English. The third one in Serbian. Yes, if you could just set it right and zoom in a bit. In English it's probably the second page. Just a moment, please. Yes. In the second quarter, it's the third one from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this second quarter? Why was a state of emergency proclaimed or declared?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was combat, JNA units, or rather, the Serb army units against Muslim formations. So the work of the public security station was conducted under quite different conditions, or rather, war time conditions, which were reflected in the fact that policemen were called upon to disarm people, search, and mop-up the terrain, protect facilities and institutions of vital importance, maintain public law and order, and bring in and interview extremists and members of paramilitary units who had taken part in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can keep this page in English but could we have the next one in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph in English it says the different interests of the above-mention parties. And in Serbian it is the fourth line in the second paragraph, loss of control and the right to look into some undesirable and unlawful conduct. How did this affect the situation, was this noted by you and Brown, your reports? What kind of effect did loss of control have, loss of control over processes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loss of control over developments and processes means the generation, or rather, the increase literally of chaos, an increase in problems, creating conditions whereby the situation can be kept under control with great difficulty in everyday situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, please, both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This last paragraph in the Serbian version, now I will try to identify it in English. Could you take a look at this, yes. [In English] Order, situation. And here there's the last paragraph, can you just take a look at this and what the police is saying, why they could not control processes and which are the villages that they are mentioning as places where it was impossible to establish law and order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief is reporting here that in the villages of Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, Domisevici, Okros - now what is this, Modra? - and some other locations, that there were activities there in that area and conflicts with the Green Berets, or rather, armed formations of the Muslims, and the police did not manage to exercise full control there in the area of public law and order because they, or rather, the Muslim forces have this area under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In English it is the penultimate paragraph, "it is important to note ..." thank you. So now let us go two pages ahead in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another one, another one, please. Page 5 in English. [In English] "Most of the work ..." [Interpretation] That's the required part in English on the fifth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this paragraph. These 11 rifles and then other hunting rifles, pistols, et cetera. What -- who was this taken away from? Actually, it says "much of the work."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is stated here that in this period, and now all of this is being listed in terms of quarters, a certain number of weapons of all kinds were taken away; that is to say, hunting weapons and pistols. But also we see some military rifles there as well. So they were taken away from all of those who possess them illegally or unlawfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there a differentiation there in terms of the ethnic background of these different citizens?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is information that provides the total of persons from whom these weapons were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go one page ahead in Serbian, then another one -- actually, page 6 in Serbian. Page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here there is a description of a critical period and of some critical events. The third paragraph in English -- or actually the fourth one in English, "in the second quarter ..." What happened there? How many persons were brought in? How many persons were released and how many persons were kept in custody?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report about a different line of work that the police are involved in. We had public law and order first, and now we have operative work which continued in different groups; that is to say, where there was grouping, where certain groups are being established. And, quite simply, there is discovery, or rather, there is work with persons who figured prominently in a negative sense in terms of how they acted. 1.030 persons were brought into custody during that period by the service and 811 of them were dealt with and currently 219 were being processed. So after they were processed some of them were released, whereas this other part, that is to say those who were assumed to have participated in combat or who were suspected of having done that, it's the majority of them, about 150 [as interpreted], they were transported, or rather -- actually, they were taken to the POW camp in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please note that in the translation these 130 were allowed to go home, home, and you were asked why they were not allowed to go home. Was it possible for them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- to be released while they were in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, I don't know if it's a translation issue. It was read out -- sorry. "... whereas this other part, that is to say those who were assumed to have participated in combat or were suspected of having done that." That's not what the document we just read from said. It says: "About 850 individuals who had taken part in combat operations or had fled from places where combat operations were being conducted ..." So just what the witness read out doesn't match what we have in English. I don't know if there's an error there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard the witness say 850 -- 811.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you start reading from "Of the 1.030 ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Of the 1.030 individuals brought in by this service and other organs (the army, the TO), 811 individuals were processed and 219 individuals are still undergoing this procedure. On completion of this process, 130 individuals were released, while 850 individuals who had taken part in combat operations or had fled from places where combat operations were being conducted are now at the Manjaca camp, where the operatives and national security employees who are processing the above-mentioned individuals also go."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me where these 130 individuals were released to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were let go home, to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, excuse me, it was represented before that that's what the document said and is the witness now saying it says that or just that he knows it from something not in the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While following this exercise, I was struggling how -- where we are going. The witness is just reading out the documents and then now he adds something. If you could assist us, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, in the English translation the words "released to go home" has been omitted. It is there in the English and people were not just let go at Manjaca to roam about, but they were taken home. So this word "home" is important. It isn't simply released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm what Mr. Karadzic said, Mr. Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the document reads "released to go home," that's what the document says in Serbian or B/C/S, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit D3911. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, just for the record it's cited at footnote 85 -- 584 in Mr. Brown's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now get 1D4217.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A short while ago it was said that the investigators are also going to Manjaca to help out with the investigations. Please tell us what this document dated 2 July is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a daily report of the operative team from the POW camp of Manjaca. It speaks about 18 POWs from Kljuc and Sanski Most being processed on that day. They say that the persons from Kljuc are nearing the end of their processing and that the process will be continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this following paragraph about Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day the processing of persons from the Sanski Most municipality began for which purpose three operatives from the public security station of that municipality have arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does Mr. Brown's report and your report respectively, how do they assess placing people at Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Brown said himself that the Manjaca camp had been established earlier by the JNA and that persons were taken there. What was pointed out, what he lays special emphasis on, was the fact that the people at Manjaca were simply picked up after some municipal attacks and taken to the camp indiscriminately. Without denying individual incidents or some undesirable conduct, there was a problem with the registering of people, their accommodation, their processing, and so on, which later all affected their status.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the second line of this paragraph, we read: "The filing of criminal complaints against persons who deserve it." What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operatives continued the activities that they had engaged on in the municipalities because they knew the situation and they knew the people. They continued documenting their acts that were illegal, and once they completed that job they would file criminal complaints against them with the courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3912, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, we do have a translation, so no objection to it coming in, in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll do so then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it in full.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the cross-examination based on document P3740 you saw the remarks that an officer at Manjaca sent out to the field about people having been taken there who had not taken part and so on. Did that document contain any evidence to that effect? Was it established somehow that they did not participate apart from their own statements?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the report of the operative team. I think that report was based on preliminary interviews that the team had conducted with the people taken to Manjaca and their statements about where they had been and what they had done. Based on that the report was drafted. I did not see the comparison of facts in -- stated by the person -- those persons and by those stated in the reports of operatives in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you as an expert tell us who is this man from Manjaca who sends out documents to the field? Is he also part of the official structures, the authorities? Who does he work for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can anyone help me? I don't know if we -- if these documents were admitted -- oh, yes, they were. Thank you. Can we now get 1D42 -- 4527.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have just mentioned that Mr. Brown suggested or put forward his opinion on how people were caught and indiscriminately sent to the camp, but tell us what you found out in the documents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a certain number of persons was collected and brought in, I saw in some documents that those for whom there were no indications that they had done anything illegal were released to go home, as we saw in the previous document, whereas those about whom there was information that they were involved in some illegal activity were taken from their respective municipalities to the Manjaca camp but there were also documents showing that their operative processing was done by the police in their municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber what this document is and why these four Muslims were sent to Manjaca. Please read the reading and the subheading.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are persons sent to the Manjaca camp for further processing. Its official name was POW camp, and with each name we see a statement of reasons why they were sent there and kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it then clearer to the investigators at Manjaca in which direction they should move and did you find any documents at Manjaca where the investigators complain of belated information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would happen that people were sent before the accompanying documents arrived. In other words, the document were sometimes late and that gave rise to dilemmas with the camp management.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a hunch that Mr. Nicholls might have a translation of this document, but at any rate I would like to tender it for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3913 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you were asked, and I'll give you a page reference too when I find it, you were asked questions about the Velagici crimes - that is page 83 - on the first day. Eighty civilians were killed. Was it clearly established that they were civilians? Was that beyond dispute? Was it always easy to establish? Of course a captured soldier mustn't be killed either, but are we sure that those people were civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see documents which would prove beyond any doubt that they were civilians. Most often - which was also confirmed by Mr. Brown - in the enclave of Vesici around 450 Muslim combatants were rounded up. And together with some of the civilian population that had not left the municipality of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I am referring to Velagici. I may have misspoken perhaps.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be my mistake as well. I heard Velagici but then I started talking about Vesici in Kotor Varos municipality. In Velagici there are no documents that would prove beyond any doubt those people were civilians. There are only documents that indicate that the incident happened after the attack on the check-point which was in the vicinity of the school in Velagici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 84 you were told that they were tried only after the year 2000 and that many had not been remanded in custody. When we're talking about the Krajina Corps or the military police, where did their role stop? What were they supposed to do in order to meet their obligations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I have to say because he's calling his expert here and putting to him that there were no documents to show that the Velagici victims were civilians, P03513 is the request for an investigation in that case, it's in evidence, the Defence has it. I think they almost have an obligation to show that to their witness now given his answer. And it's page 2 of the B/C/S makes it very clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell the crux of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, well it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The request for an investigation states: "On the 1st of June, 1992, a group of 80 civilians were brought to the check-point in the village of Velagici ..." And then goes on to talk about here these are the 80 people who were shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Having heard Mr. Nicholls' submission, would you like to add anything, Mr. Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't remember that I have seen that request for investigation. However, if that is what it says, I said that I didn't see any documents that would prove beyond any reasonable doubt that those were only civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, that's not his role to say whether the documents prove anything beyond reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Nicholls spoke about 65 ter 15941 which is now in evidence as P --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karadzic might want to ask his expert witness what Article 142 is, which is what the soldiers were charged with in this case. Article 142 is war crimes against civilians. That's what the Velagici massacre suspects were charged with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at 65 ter 15941 in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Other articles are mentioned there, 157 and 158. I believe that we are talking about the law on filing a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Nicholls be of assistance and tell me whether this is the document in question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please tell us what happens once a request for investigation is filed, i.e., once a criminal report is filed? What is the role of the corps after that? Under whose authorities they fall after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that they fall under the authority of the court and the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was said that before they were put on trial, they were not remanded in custody. Could you please tell us what is it that regulates the remand in custody? Does it -- can it be endless or is there a regulation with that regard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an investigative judge who orders for a person to be remanded in custody and for how long. I'm not sure that I am familiar with articles of the act that regulate the length of that remand, but I know that at that time the military police could only keep suspects for a day.
